results.title: HNSW: Navigating the Metric Lattice
results.content: Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs are a popular approximate nearest neighbour index. The HNSW paper describes a multi-layer graph that routes queries from coarse to fine layers, giving logarithmic search complexity for high-dimensional vectors. Because every layer is itself a navigable small world, an insertion only needs to connect to a constant number of neighbours per layer, which keeps index build time linear in the number of vectors while search stays logarithmic in practice.

results.title: Benchmarking vector indexes in production
results.content: Latency and recall benchmarks compare HNSW, IVF and brute-force scans on real workloads. Recall@10 with a probe of 32 is a common operating point; memory budget and index build time decide the winner. The benchmark should report both p95 latency and recall because an index that is fast but misses relevant documents is worse than a slower exact scan for small collections.

results.title: BM25 full-text search primer
results.content: BM25 ranks documents by term frequency with length normalisation and a saturation k1 parameter. It remains a strong lexical baseline and is often combined with dense retrieval in hybrid search pipelines. The score of a document is a sum over query terms of idf-weighted saturations, so rare terms contribute more than frequent ones and long documents are penalised for their length.

results.title: Hybrid search: dense plus sparse
results.content: Hybrid search fuses a dense vector retriever with a sparse lexical ranker, then merges the two result lists. Reciprocal rank fusion is the simplest merge that is robust to score scale differences. Dense retrieval handles synonyms and paraphrases, sparse retrieval handles exact identifiers and rare tokens, and the fusion step combines both strengths into a single ranked list.

results.title: Embedding models for retrieval
results.content: Modern embedding models map text into fixed-size vectors so that semantic similarity becomes cosine distance. Multilingual models keep a single index for several languages at a small quality cost. The choice of dimensionality trades memory against precision: 256 dimensions are enough for many corpora, while larger models push the useful dimension count into the thousands.

results.title: Evaluating retrieval with recall@k
results.content: Recall@k measures how often the relevant document appears in the top k results. Golden query sets with expected fragments gate regressions before a search change is released. The gate should use a fixed, versioned set of queries with fragments that exist verbatim in the corpus, so the metric stays reproducible between rebuilds and across developers.

results.title: Approximate nearest neighbour tradeoffs
results.content: Approximate indexes trade a little recall for a large speedup. The number of probes and the graph connectivity control the balance, and both should be tuned on the target corpus. More probes improve recall linearly at first and then flatten, while wider graphs increase the memory footprint, so the operating point depends on the hardware budget.

results.title: Cypher queries on a property graph
results.content: Cypher is the declarative query language of property graphs. A graph hop follows typed relationships, for example from a file to the commit that last changed it. Property graphs store nodes and relationships with attributes, which makes them a natural fit for provenance chains where each hop adds a timestamped actor to the history of a document.

results.title: Embedded databases for local-first tools
results.content: An embedded database lives inside the application process: no server, one file, ACID transactions. Local-first tools use them to keep user data on the device and index it offline. Because there is no network round trip, writes commit in microseconds, and the whole knowledge base can be copied by copying a single file to another machine.

results.title: Serving search over HTTP and MCP
results.content: A small HTTP surface with health, search and stats endpoints is enough for agents to query a local brain. An MCP tool wrapper maps the same endpoints to model-callable tools. Keeping the tool list minimal matters: every exposed tool is a capability an agent may invoke, so search and audit belong, while internal maintenance endpoints stay behind the operator interface.
